description: The heart of the database. These questions ask a professional to make tacit knowledge explicit - the thing they know how to do but have never had to put into words. They work across industries because every field has novices, masters, and a gap between them, even when the content of the gap is completely different.

questions.text: What separates someone with five years in from someone with twenty? Be specific - what can the twenty-year person actually do?
questions.lands_because: Forces expertise into observable behavior instead of adjectives. The demand for specificity is doing the work - without it you get 'experience' and 'judgment' and nothing else.
followups: Can that be taught, or does it only come from repetition?
Is there anything the five-year person does better?

questions.text: What can you tell in the first ten minutes of a {work_unit} that a novice could not tell in a week?
questions.lands_because: Rapid pattern recognition is the signature of expertise in every field. Fill the slot from the industry profile - case, job, matter, load, story, service - and it sounds native.
followups: What are you actually looking at when you make that read?

questions.text: What part of your job could you do exhausted, and what part genuinely requires you to be sharp?
questions.lands_because: Separates automated skill from live cognition, which is a distinction professionals feel acutely and are almost never invited to describe.
followups: What happens when you have to do the sharp part while exhausted anyway?

setting_text.entrepreneur: What part of running this could you do exhausted, and what genuinely requires you to be sharp?

questions.text: What is the hardest thing in your field to teach?
questions.lands_because: Points straight at the tacit core of the craft. Guests who train others have thought about this constantly and have examples ready.
followups: Who taught it to you well?

questions.text: What is a rule everyone is taught that good people in your field break?
questions.lands_because: Gets at the difference between procedure and practice. The guest has to trust you before answering honestly, so place it after they have warmed up.
followups: How do you know when you have earned the right to break it?
What happens to someone who breaks it too early?
questions.avoid_if: The guest works under a regulator or licensing body and the honest answer could expose them. Offer the escape hatch: 'or a rule you would keep but that people argue about.'

questions.text: Teach me one thing from your field I could actually use tomorrow.
questions.lands_because: Turns the guest into a teacher, which is a comfortable and generous posture, and gives the audience a concrete takeaway to remember the episode by.
followups: What do people usually get wrong when they try that?

questions.text: How do you know when a {work_unit} is finished? Who actually decides?
questions.lands_because: Completion is contested in almost every profession - good enough versus perfect, and whether the decision belongs to the practitioner, the client, or the clock.
followups: When was the last time you disagreed with that call?

questions.text: What do you notice about your {customer} that they have no idea you are noticing?
questions.lands_because: Every professional reads their counterpart for signals - a patient's gait, a client's hesitation, a buyer's questions, a room's energy. It feels like letting the audience behind the glass.
followups: What does the signal usually mean?

questions.text: Is there a piece of your work you are quietly proud of that nobody would ever notice?
questions.lands_because: Invisible excellence is nearly universal - the clean wire run behind the drywall, the paragraph nobody had to reread, the handoff that prevented an incident. Warm and revealing at once.

setting_text.entrepreneur: Is there a piece of your work you are quietly proud of that no client would ever notice?

questions.text: What does your field consider a good day, and do you agree with that definition?
questions.lands_because: The second half is the whole question. It opens a gap between institutional metrics and personal standards without asking the guest to attack their employer.

setting_text.entrepreneur: What counts as a good day in your business, and do you agree with that definition?
